topic: building a dished rear wheel for a touring bike: spoke tension, the valve hole and truing

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: miernik naprezenia szprych

base: I am building a rear wheel for a touring bike and lacing it three cross both sides.
The front wheel from the same build sits finished on the bench and runs beautifully true.
A tension meter came with the stand, though I have barely learned to read it yet.
The rear wheel goes true easily enough, but the spokes feel very different side to side.
Is that difference expected, or have I laced something wrong on the drive side?
That difference is expected, because the drive side sits at a much steeper angle.
A dished rear wheel always carries far more tension on the side nearest the sprockets.
The left spokes will feel slack by comparison even when the wheel is perfectly built.
Judge the drive side by the meter and let the left side fall where it must.
I brought the drive side up gradually and the wheel is round within half a millimetre.
The tension meter reads fairly evenly across the drive spokes, apart from two loose ones.
Those two sit either side of the valve hole, which cannot be a coincidence surely.
The front wheel showed nothing similar when I built it a fortnight ago in July.
Is the rim faulty there, or does the valve hole always cause this kind of trouble?
The valve hole is always the weak spot, since there is no spoke hole beside it.
Rims flex slightly there and two neighbouring spokes end up carrying an easier life.
Bring them up to match the rest and check the roundness again very carefully afterwards.
A rim that stays out of round only at the valve is usually simply rather tired.
I evened the two spokes and the whole drive side now reads within ten percent.
The wheel is true sideways and round to about a third of a millimetre.
It still pings loudly whenever I lean on it, which sounds alarming to me.
Should I stress the wheel harder, or is that noise a sign of something wrong?
Stress it harder, because pinging is only the spokes settling into the hub flanges.
Grip pairs of spokes and squeeze firmly all the way around, then true it again.
Repeat that until the wheel stays quiet and the truing no longer changes anything.
A wheel that never pings has usually been built too slack to last very long.
Three rounds of squeezing quieted it and the truing stopped moving after the second.
The dish is slightly out now, about a millimetre towards the drive side.
I would rather not disturb the tension I have just balanced across the drive spokes.
Can I correct the dish from the left side alone, or must I touch both?
Correct it from the left alone, since that side has tension to spare anyway.
Loosen every left spoke by an eighth of a turn and the rim will move over.
Work right around the wheel in one direction so nothing is left behind.
Then check the drive tension once more, because it always drifts slightly during that move.
The dish came right after one full pass and the drive tension barely moved at all.
The wheel has done three hundred miles now, loaded, and has stayed perfectly true.
One left spoke sounds a lower note than its neighbours when I pluck the spokes.
Is that worth chasing, or should I leave a wheel alone once it settles properly?
Leave it alone, because chasing one note usually spoils a wheel that already works.
Note differs with spoke length and lacing, so plucking tells you less than people claim.
Check the rim for cracks around the eyelets once a season and nothing more.
A wheel that survives three hundred loaded miles unchanged will very likely last for years.
